title: Competing risks: the cumulative incidence function
summary: Estimates how many patients actually have the event, when a competing event can stop them from ever having it.

sizing._why: There is no closed form in the catalog for a cumulative incidence comparison, and borrowing the log-rank form would size a different quantity. Gray's test has its own literature; sizing one is a simulation.

_this_is_the_entry_the_others_point_at: CLAUDE.md's statistical rules name this failure directly: where death competes with the event of interest, a Kaplan-Meier curve is not merely off-message, it censors the competing death and overstates cumulative incidence. This entry is that error with numbers on it, and it computes the wrong estimator alongside the right one so the gap is in the output.
_no_effect_measure: summaryMeasure is `other`: this estimates a CURVE. A subdistribution hazard ratio is Fine-Gray and a cause-specific hazard ratio is a Cox model on cause 1 with cause 2 censored -- different questions, both out of scope here.
pinned_defaults: R: status as a FACTOR in Surv(), which makes it a multi-state fit and gives Aalen-Johansen. Surv(time, status) with a numeric status counts EVERY non-zero code as the event; Surv(time, status == 1) censors the competing cause. Three spellings, three answers, no warning.
Python: AalenJohansenFitter with event_of_interest=1, taking the FULL status column. Passing a 0/1 indicator makes the competing cause censoring and returns the naive curve under a different name.
SAS: eventcode=1 on PROC LIFETEST. Without it the same procedure returns a Kaplan-Meier curve; time*status(0 2) is a third spelling that censors cause 2.
Stata: stcompet ... , compet1(2). The stset declares status 1 the failure, which alone would make status 2 censoring.
Every file also computes the NAIVE curve on purpose, so the size of the error is in the output rather than in a comment.
